idiom_name: visitor class with non-pure virtual defaults + dynamic_cast capability cross-cast
implementation_notes: The classic home of the pattern: the visitor is a class rather than an interface, and its per-element visit overloads have non-pure virtual bodies, so extending an operation means deriving from an existing visitor and inheriting its behaviour for the elements it already handles. A new element kind derives from an intermediate base whose accept overload takes the extended visitor and reaches it with a sideways cast - `dynamic_cast<UnionVisitor*>(&v)` - falling back to the base default when the cast fails; cppreference documents the cross-cast and its requirement that the source type be polymorphic. C++ has no virtual constructors, so an operation that needs another visitor during traversal must build it through a virtual factory such as `clone()`. Reach for this structure only when the element set is open across binaries: with a fixed set, std::variant plus std::visit gives compile-time exhaustiveness and no RTTI, at the price of editing the variant to add a type.
pitfalls: A non-pure virtual visit makes a missing case a runtime event: forgetting `= 0` on a slot you really require turns a compile error into a silent default or an exception at the first element.

dynamic_cast needs RTTI and a polymorphic source type - it is unavailable with -fno-rtti, and the cross-cast is well defined only when the visitor actually derives from the extended interface; a static_cast there is undefined behaviour instead of a failed probe.

Self-construction during traversal must go through a virtual factory; `new Eval(...)` inside a visitor loses every subclass's extension one level down, which is the flaw the C# write-up documents for recursive types.
The probe must handle `nullptr`/failed casts explicitly: a visitor that does not implement the extended interface is normal, not an error, so the fallback path has to be the well-defined one.
